chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Mahboub, from Ali ibn Ri'ab, from Zurara, who said:

Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) attended the funeral of a man from Quraish, and I was with him, and Ata'a was among them. A woman shrieked, and Ata'a said to her, 'Will you be quiet or shall we return?' He said, so she did not be quiet, so Ata'a returned. I said to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), 'Indeed, Ata'a has returned.' He said, 'And why?' I said, 'This woman shrieked, so he said to her, 'Will you be quiet or shall we return?' But she did not be quiet, so he returned.' He (Abu Ja'far) said, 'Proceed with us. For if we, when we see something of falsehood along with the Truth, were to leave the Truth for it, we would not fulfill the right of a Muslim.'

He (the narrator) said, 'So when he had prayed over the funeral, its guardian said to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), 'Return, having been recompensed, may Allah have mercy on you, for you are not strong enough for walking.' But he refused to return. I said to him, 'He has permitted you to return, and I have a need which I want to ask you about.' He said, 'Proceed. For it is not by his permission that we came, nor is it by his permission that we return. Rather, it is a merit and a reward that we sought. For according to what the man follows the funeral, the man is recompensed for that.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling and etiquette on following a funeral procession and the associated reward?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi highlights Imam al-Baqir’s (as) steadfastness in fulfilling the Sunnah of following the funeral procession, demonstrating that the reward is intrinsic to the act of following rather than contingent on the family's permission or external distractions like the woman's crying. It underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on consistency in ritual practice (Mu'atabah) and the spiritual merit derived from accompanying the deceased until burial, regardless of social interruptions.
